result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.tensor_product()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the tensor (categorical, Kronecker) product of this graph with another. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L29476-L29539){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.tensor_product(other) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Tensor product](/assets/graphs/tensor-product.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="G is a triangle A, B, C (accent edges) and H is a single edge 0–1 (teal). In the tensor product both coordinates must move along an edge at once, so every product edge is ink: (A, 0)–(B, 1), (B, 1)–(C, 0), and so on, labeled A0 to C1. The result has 6 nodes and 6 edges forming a single 6-cycle, the bipartite double cover of the triangle." width="100%"} The tensor product $G \times H$ has a node for every pair `(g, h)`, and joins `(g, h)` to `(g', h')` when `g`-`g'` is an edge of this graph *and* `h`-`h'` is an edge of `other`: both coordinates must move at once. Its adjacency matrix is the Kronecker product of the two adjacency matrices, which is why Kronecker graph models of real networks are built from repeated tensor products of a small seed graph. A classic fact: the tensor product of a graph with a single edge is its bipartite double cover. Both graphs must be directed or both undirected. If either graph is weighted, each product edge's weight is the product of the two factor weights. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [other]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The second factor. Neither graph is modified. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with `n * m` nodes, numbered and labeled as in `cartesian_product()`. Edge attributes become tuples `(value of the edge in this graph, value in other)`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If one graph is directed and the other is not. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} For undirected graphs each pair of edges `g-g'` and `h-h'` yields the two product edges `(g, h)-(g', h')` and `(g', h)-(g, h')`, so there are $2|E_G||E_H|$ edges (fewer when self-loops make the two coincide). The eigenvalues of the product are all products of an eigenvalue of each factor. Results match NetworkX's `tensor_product`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The tensor product of a triangle with a single edge is a 6-cycle, the bipartite double cover of the triangle: ::: {#10880087 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec triangle = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) triangle.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")]) edge = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["0", "1"]).add_edge("0", "1") cover = triangle.tensor_product(edge) cover.count_edges(), cover.is_isomorphic(ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(6)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (6, True) ``` ::: ::: With weights, every product edge carries the product of its two factor weights: ::: {#e1cabaa8 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} a = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B"]).add_edge("A", "B", weight=2.0) b = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["x", "y"]).add_edge("x", "y", weight=3.0) [a.tensor_product(b).get_edge(e).weight for e in a.tensor_product(b).get_edge_ids()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` [6.0, 6.0] ``` ::: :::
